deep_dive_html:
The Perils of Discretionary Relocation

In a commercial dental lease, a standard relocation clause is a latent liability that can dismantle a practice's profitability. Landlords frequently draft these provisions with "sole discretion" language, granting them the unilateral right to move your practice to any available space within the center. While the square footage might remain nominally identical, the functional utility of the new space is often drastically inferior, particularly regarding specialized medical infrastructure.

For dental practitioners, the danger lies in the "comparable space" ambiguity. A landlord may argue that a suite with the same footprint is "comparable," even if the new location lacks the necessary plumbing density, electrical capacity for heavy machinery, or the high-visibility frontage essential for patient acquisition. If the lease does not strictly define the technical parameters of the replacement space, you are essentially signing a blank check for a costly and disruptive clinic reconfiguration.

Establishing Technical Minimums

To mitigate this risk, a lease must move beyond vague descriptions and establish rigorous, objective criteria for any potential relocation. An elite-level negotiation focuses on "Permissible Replacement Space" standards that prioritize clinical continuity over mere footprint equivalence. You must ensure the lease mandates that any relocated space meets the following criteria:

  • Utility Parity: Explicit requirements for plumbing, compressed air, and electrical load capacities that mirror the original premises.
  • Visibility and Signage: Guaranteed visibility levels and the right to maintain equivalent signage prominence to prevent patient attrition.
  • Build-out Indemnification: A mandate that the landlord bears 100% of the costs for all structural and mechanical modifications required for the move.
  • Right of Refusal: The tenant's absolute right to reject any space that fails to meet the pre-defined technical specifications.

Failure to audit these clauses during the lease inception phase can lead to catastrophic capital expenditures and operational downtime.
